questions.question: Which AI model actually performs best on needle-in-haystack tests for long documents?
questions.answer_summary: Real HN discussion: Gemini models (from 1.5 onward) show near-perfect recall on needle-in-haystack tests; Claude 3 Opus shows sensitivity to where information is placed in long inputs; Llama 4 claims 10M token context with demonstrated needle-finding.

questions.question: Does a huge advertised context window (1M+ tokens) mean the model actually understands the whole document?
questions.answer_summary: HN commenters disagree sharply: one calls Gemini 2.0's 1M-context PDF ingestion 'hopeless' beyond ~20-40k tokens with real degradation, while another calls Gemini 2.5's long-context handling a 'breakthrough moment' versus older models that 'get lost, hallucinate and are pretty much worthless' past 200k tokens.

questions.question: Why does model performance degrade well before the advertised context limit is reached?
questions.answer_summary: A real user report found a model 'works okay out to roughly 20-40k tokens' but 'degrades significantly' beyond that threshold, despite a much larger advertised window, and found GPT-4o better than the tested alternative under 128k tokens.

questions.question: Is it better to paste a whole document/codebase into context, or use RAG/GraphRAG chunking?
questions.answer_summary: HN examples split both ways: one developer built a GraphRAG-based PR reviewer specifically to 'work around context window limitations,' while another commenter reports direct full-context inclusion outperforming RAG for architectural understanding.

questions.question: Does the language of the document change the effective cost/efficiency of long-document analysis across models?
questions.answer_summary: A concrete tokenizer comparison on HN found Claude Sonnet 4.5 encodes Tamil at 1.19 chars/token versus Gemini's 4.24 chars/token — roughly a 3.5x cost difference for equivalent non-English document content.

questions.question: Does GPT's larger advertised context window (400k) actually hold up better than Claude's 200k in sustained real use?
questions.answer_summary: One HN comment claims GPT-5 offers a 'reliable 400k window' versus Claude's '200k hard limit' for sustained coding/document sessions, though this is a single practitioner's account, not a controlled benchmark.

questions.question: Why do models seem to get 'lazier' about actually reading long documents rather than skimming?
questions.answer_summary: An HN commenter frames the needle-in-haystack benchmark itself as testing 'how lazy is my LLM being when it comes to analyzing the input I've provided to it,' distinguishing surface retrieval from genuine reading.

questions.question: What's the difference between a model's 'physical' and 'effective' context window?
questions.answer_summary: HN discussion distinguishes the marketed 'physical' token limit from the smaller 'effective context window' the model can actually use accurately, with proprietary filtering discarding seemingly irrelevant tokens.

questions.question: Do models struggle more with simple retrieval or with complex reasoning over long documents?
questions.answer_summary: HN commenters note models handle simple 'needle' retrieval fairly well but 'struggle with complex reasoning over lengthy contexts' — the benchmark only reveals surface-level capability, not deep comprehension.

questions.question: Can models handle sustained 300k+ token sessions in real coding/document work?
questions.answer_summary: A developer reports coding sessions reaching 'about 350k tokens long' and argues a model capped at 200k 'really isn't a sophisticated enough model' for that kind of sustained document/code work.

questions.question: Why might a condensed 'skill' file work better than pasting a full long document into context?
questions.answer_summary: A real example: a 55,000-word guide was 'too big for a context window' to get coherent answers from directly, so the author condensed it into a separate skill/reference file with key frameworks instead.

questions.question: Which models do practitioners actually reach for when summarizing documents day-to-day?
questions.answer_summary: HN commenters mention Gemini and ChatGPT as 'fairly well behaved' for summarization, with budget alternatives (Llama 4, Qwen, GLM) seen as 'okay/not bad' but not top-tier, suggesting choice is often driven by budget as much as capability.
